title: Forwards and swaps: fixed against floating
story: Thursday. Robin draws two lines on the whiteboard. *"NS-01 is priced on Dated Brent, but our hedge is in Brent futures. Close, but not the same price. Many desks use a swap on Dated Brent instead: no exchange, no daily margin, and the same price as the cargo."* Chris shrugs: *"Swap, future, I just want the price locked."*
objective: I can explain a forward and a fixed-for-floating swap, and calculate a simple swap settlement.

write.heading: 1. Forward
write.body: A **forward** is an OTC deal (→ L18) to buy or sell at a fixed price on a future date. It is tailored, not cleared, and settled only at the end. Example: 600,000 bbl for March delivery.

write.heading: 2. Swap
write.body:
A **swap** exchanges a **fixed price** against a **floating price**, typically the average of a published price (→ L9) over a period. There is no delivery: only the difference is paid in cash.
**Settlement = (floating - fixed) × volume**, paid to the fixed-price payer if positive.

write.heading: 3. A swap on NS-01
write.body:
Northbridge **sells** a Dated Brent swap: it receives fixed and pays floating (→ L20).
Example: fixed 80 USD/bbl, average Dated Brent 78 USD/bbl, 600,000 bbl.
Northbridge receives (80 - 78) × 600,000 = **1,200,000 USD**. The cargo lost value, the swap paid it back.

write.heading: 4. Middle office check
write.body: Check the **direction** (who pays fixed), the floating index, the averaging period and the volume. A wrong sign turns a hedge into a double bet.

check.q: What is exchanged in a fixed-for-floating swap?
check.a: A fixed price against a floating price (the average of a published index over a period). Only the cash difference is paid, there is no physical delivery.

check.q: Northbridge receives fixed 80 and pays floating. The average is 78 on 600,000 bbl. Who pays, and how much?
Give two differences between a swap and a future (→ L24).
check.a: A future is a standard exchange contract, cleared, with daily margin. A swap is typically OTC, tailored (any index, period and volume), with bilateral credit risk and cash settlement at the end of the period.

read_more: Oil swaps are usually priced against the average of a PRA assessment (for example Platts Dated Brent) over a month or another agreed period. Many OTC swaps can also be cleared through an exchange clearing house, which then removes the bilateral credit risk; cleared OTC comes back in module 7. The small difference between the price of the cargo (Dated Brent) and the price of the hedge (Brent futures) is called basis risk, a topic for lesson 33. All prices, volumes and the choice of a swap for NS-01 are illustrative, part of the fictional story.
next: Next lesson (L26): pricing periods: why NS-01 may be priced on the average of five days around the bill of lading.
